title: Wendell and the Songbook
premise: Wendell Osei, a ghostwriter who has spent twelve years hiding behind other people's stories, is hired to pen the memoirs of festival director Marcus Hale — and discovers in Marcus's papers a letter he wrote eleven years ago and never sent, to the woman who left him without a word. The letter pulls him back toward Ada Kavanagh, now a music teacher returning for the town's centennial festival, where Marcus intends to premiere the memoir and the truth it contains about the night that separated them. As Wendell and Ada piece together what really happened — and Marcus's polished version threatens to bury it — Wendell must choose between the safe, borrowed life he has built and the whole, unguarded heart the festival's final night demands. He chooses truth: he reads the unsent letter aloud at the closing concert, and Ada answers with a song she has carried for eleven years.
about_author: L. M. Okonkwo is the pen name of a former session cellist who traded orchestra pits for quiet rooms and manuscripts, writing love stories about people who communicate better on paper than in person. They live in a coastal town that holds one festival a year and never quite lets anyone leave.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Voice
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A ghostwriter who has perfected disappearing accepts the commission to write festival director Marcus Hale's memoirs, telling himself it's just another job. In Marcus's cluttered archive he glimpses a familiar handwriting on an old envelope. Emotional beat: the unease of a man who has made safety his craft sensing danger.

chapters.title: Postmarked Eleven Years Ago
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Sorting boxes, Wendell finds his own unsent letter — the one he wrote to Ada the night she vanished — in Marcus's files, with a note in Marcus's hand: 'Hold until the memoir.' Panic and longing collide as he realizes Marcus knew Ada's story all along. Emotional beat: the past arriving with a return address.

chapters.title: Ada, Tuning
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada returns to town to rehearse the centennial concert, telling herself twelve years and one ocean have settled everything. She hears Wendell's name on the festival roster and her hands go flat on the keys. Emotional beat: memory as muscle memory — the body remembering what the mind has filed away.

chapters.title: Small Safe Steps
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wendell and Ada meet by accident at the bandstand and conduct a careful, witty, devastatingly polite conversation, both performing composure. That night Wendell rereads the unsent letter and cannot decide whether to confess or destroy it. Emotional beat: two people fluent in retreat, testing the first step.

chapters.title: What Marcus Knew
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell confronts Marcus, who admits he intercepted the letter years ago to protect Ada — or so he claims — and that the memoir's centerpiece chapter tells 'the whole Kavanagh story' as he remembers it. Wendell realizes the book will publish a version of events that is loyal to Marcus but false. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth splitting down the middle.

chapters.title: The Night We Don't Talk About
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada and Wendell finally speak of the night she left: her father's ultimatum, the job abroad, the letter she waited for that never came. The unsent letter's existence reframes everything — she left believing silence was his answer. Emotional beat: grief and fury braided together, the first honest touch in twelve years.

chapters.title: Advance Copy
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A galley of the memoir leaks to the festival committee; Ada reads Marcus's chapter, which casts her departure as abandonment and Wendell's silence as indifference. Feeling doubly betrayed — by Marcus's version and by Wendell's complicity — she withdraws from the concert. Emotional beat: the cost of lending pieces of the heart instead of risking the whole.

chapters.title: The Draft That Tells the Truth
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wendell writes the memoir's final chapter himself — not Marcus's version, but the true one — and gives Ada the only copy, asking nothing. Marcus threatens to fire him and bury the chapter; Wendell signs away the credit instead. Emotional beat: choosing truth over the safe career, the first whole-hearted act.

chapters.title: Closing Night
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. At the centennial's final concert, Marcus premieres the memoir as written; Wendell walks onstage during intermission and reads the unsent letter aloud to a full house, claiming every word as his own failure and his own love. Emotional beat: the climax — public vulnerability as the only honest stage left.

chapters.title: The Songbook
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada answers from the stage with the song she wrote the night she left, then the one she finished after hearing the letter — eleven years of music given whole. In the emptied bandstand afterward, they begin again without borrowed words. Epilogue beat: a life no longer measured in small safe steps, but in duets.
